source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning, Study 1 (original paper, full text)
finding: Twenty CMU undergraduates learned BigTrak, then had to find how the RPT key works. 19 of 20 found it. They split by how they left the wrong 'N is a counter' frame: 13 Experimenters (found it by running a region-III experiment) and 7 Theorists (found it by searching memory for a new frame).
numbers: N=20; 364 programs, 304 were experiments. Table 5, Experimenters vs Theorists: time 24.46 vs 11.40 min (t(18)=3.97); experiments 18.33 vs 9.29 (t(18)=3.09); experiments without a stated hypothesis 6.08 vs 0.76 (t(18)=3.70); different hypotheses 4.92 vs 3.06 (ns, p<.08); hypothesis switches 4.76 vs 3.00 (ns, p<.07). Combined: 19.40 min, 15.20 experiments, 4.55 hypotheses, 4.15 switches. Experimenters ran about 6 hypothesis-free experiments before the key one.
limits: The split is 13 Experimenters to 7 Theorists. The PDF text extraction garbled one Table 5 cell (Theorists 'experiments with hypotheses' reads 0.57; the combined mean of 11.00 implies about 8.6), so do not quote that cell. One lab, one device, college students.
agent_relevance: Both routes reach the answer, but the Theorist route (new frame from memory) was twice as fast and used half the experiments. Hypothesis-first with memory search is the cheaper default; exploration of experiments is the fallback when no frame comes to mind.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Study 1, Table 4: what subjects did with confirming and disconfirming outcomes
finding: Subjects were only partly sensitive to disconfirmation. They kept a disconfirmed hypothesis in over half of the disconfirming outcomes, and dropped a confirmed one in a quarter of the confirming outcomes.
numbers: Across 220 outcomes with a stated hypothesis: 21 of 84 confirming outcomes led to rejection (25%); 76 of 136 disconfirming outcomes led to retention (56%), so only 60 of 136 (44%) led to a change. Per subject that is about 4 retained disconfirmed hypotheses and 1 abandoned confirmed hypothesis per 11 outcomes. Chi-square 8.16, p<.005 (responses not random). By group: Experimenters 17 reject-after-confirm, 43 retain-after-disconfirm, 44 reject-after-disconfirm; Theorists 4, 20, 16.
quote: in over half (76/136) of the disconfirming instances, they retain the disconfirmed hypothesis
limits: The authors give reasons for retention: feedback was sometimes wrong (memory and observe errors), subjects repeated the same experiment to check, and some encoded disconfirming results as confirming. So not all retention is stubbornness.
agent_relevance: Human baseline for anomaly handling: about half of anomalies are not acted on at once. An LLM agent is not unusual if it does the same, but it should log a retained-despite-contradiction flag so the miss is visible.

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) on Klayman and Ha: positive testing in BigTrak, Study 1 and 2 breakdown
finding: Subjects almost always used a positive test ('if BigTrak does this, my hypothesis is right'), yet about 60 percent of experiments disconfirmed the hypothesis, so positive testing still falsified. The authors say this fits Klayman and Ha: positive tests work when the chance of confirmation is small.
numbers: Study 1: 4.6 (SD 1.3) different hypotheses per subject; 55% of experiments ran under one of 8 common hypotheses, 3% under partial ones, 28% under no stated hypothesis. About 60% of experiments in Study 1 and Study 2 gave disconfirming evidence. Study 2 (10 adults, hypotheses stated first): 7 of 10 switched to the selector frame in phase 1; 5 of 10 proposed the correct rule; phase 2 all 10 solved it, mean 6.2 min, 5.7 experiments, 2.4 hypotheses. Theorists 4 (3.3 min, 3.0 experiments) vs Experimenters 6 (8.2 min, 7.5 experiments); all 4 Theorists and 1 Experimenter had programming experience.
limits: The authors note that in a Wason 2-4-6 type task, where confirmation is likely, positive tests give no information. Study 2 groups are tiny (4 and 6).
agent_relevance: Confirm-first testing is not wrong in itself. What matters is whether the hypothesis is broader or narrower than the truth. Our S7 should check that relation, not ban confirming tests.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing, Psychological Review 94:211
finding: A positive test (a case you expect to have the target property) is the better way to find a falsification when the target is a minority phenomenon and the hypothesis is about the right size. Negative tests are needed when the hypothesis is too narrow (a strict subset of the true rule). The tendency to test positive is described as widely replicated.
numbers: Their Eq. 2: if p(t)<.5 and p(h) is about p(t), the chance of falsification is higher for positive hypothesis tests than for negative ones. Examples given: prevalence of schizophrenia under 1%, AIDS incidence in the US. Tweney et al. (1980) DAX/MED feedback (rule vs everything else treated as two hypotheses) greatly raised success on the 2-4-6 task by inducing tests of both.
limits: Primary text opened. No direct failed replication of the 2-4-6 effect appears in this paper; it lists replications (Mahoney, Mynatt et al., Taplin, Tweney et al., Wason and Johnson-Laird) and says people do not follow +testing strictly when given enough test opportunities. The Wetherick 1962 and Wason 1962 exchange is cited only second-hand here.
agent_relevance: S7 test rule: judge whether the current hypothesis is likely narrower or broader than the target. If narrower (typical when starting from an example), force a negative test. If the target is rare and the hypothesis is about its size, positive tests are fine.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori and Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench, full text re-read: design and boundary condition
finding: In FalsifyBench the true rule R is a WordNet category and starting examples come from a deeper node, so the player's hypothesis H is almost always inside R. Positive tests then can never falsify, and only negative tests can. So the benchmark mostly tests the one case where confirming fails, not the rare-target case where confirming helps.
numbers: 12 models, 100 games each, 1,200 test turns. Best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%; top reasoning GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%; GPT-5-Nano 12% and Qwen3.5-9B 21% are below all instruct models. Confirmation bias (share of positive tests): reasoning 24.2% to 39.0%, instruct 66% to 82%. Spearman rho=-0.779 (p=.003) with success; rho=-0.937 (p<.001) with conclusive falsification rate (best GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, worst Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%). Bayesian logistic regression n=1,200: confirmation bias posterior mean -4.15 (OR 0.016); oracle error -0.12 (interval spans zero). H inside R in more than 50% of turns for almost all models (GPT-5.2-Chat lower).
limits: H-R relations were labelled by GPT-5-Mini, a model also tested. Each LLM played both player and oracle. Failed games had more disjoint or partial-overlap hypotheses, so part of failure is bad hypothesis generation, not only bad testing. No condition with a rare R or an H broader than R was run on purpose, so the Klayman and Ha positive-test win is untested for LLMs here.
agent_relevance: Our code-side check can label each test as positive or negative relative to the current hypothesis, but needs a way to estimate the H-R relation. Gap 10 stays open: nobody has tested LLMs where confirming should win.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify, full text re-read: intervention tables
finding: Prompts that ask for counterexamples help thinking models and are mixed for non-thinking ones. The prompts also change tokens spent per turn, so these are not equal-token comparisons. No code-forced falsifying test was run, so gap 1 is not answered here.
numbers: Table 2 (80 episodes per cell). Qwen3-32B thinking: baseline success 0.41 (I:C 0.14), Think-in-Opposites 0.61 (I:C 0.54); tokens per turn 1029.8 to 1450.0. Qwen3-32B non-thinking: baseline 0.33, TiO 0.36, Dual-Goal 0.10. Qwen3-8B thinking 0.21 to 0.36 (TiO). Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.73 to 0.78 (TiO) and 0.78 (Dual-Goal). TiO raises success in all 11 model-modes; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11; both raise I:C in 18 of 22 cases. Thinking models up to 16K tokens per turn, non-thinking 256. Distilling TiO traces: Qwen3-8B 0.21 to 0.36 (own teacher) or 0.59 (32B teacher with TiO); Qwen3-32B 0.41 to 0.64.
limits: Table text is partly garbled in extraction; Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B thinking values were cross-checked against Table 3. Same human-derived rule sets. Significance only for thinking models.
agent_relevance: Prompting costs extra tokens. A fair test of a code-forced test needs equal total tokens. We found no such test anywhere.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify: Blicket transfer and what drives thinking gains
finding: Thinking mode raises success without a steady rise in the incompatible-to-compatible test ratio, so the gain does not come mainly from choosing more falsifying tests. On the Blicket task, lower confirmation bias still tracks success, and TiO helps thinking models most.
numbers: Blicket test, 192 episodes per point: Qwen3-8B base success 0.32 (I:C 0.44), TiO 0.40 (0.57); Qwen3-32B base 0.57 (0.54), TiO 0.86 (1.31). Wason-distilled models on Blicket: Qwen3-8B 0.32 to 0.34, 0.36 or 0.38 depending on teacher; Qwen3-32B 0.57 to 0.77. Correlation of I:C with success is significant for both thinking and non-thinking models.
limits: The paper offers the observation, not a mechanism. Better inference after each test is the natural candidate but was not isolated. Gap 8 is therefore only partly closed, with RAUMA and DiscoverPhysics (d10, d17).
agent_relevance: Do not assume that more falsifying tests is the only lever. Track test choice and inference quality as separate scores.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: counterfactual law discovery, code interpreter and exploration (ICLR 2026)
finding: 324 law-discovery tasks in 12 physics domains use counterfactual shifted laws so recall cannot help. A code interpreter helps weak models but slightly hurts strong ones, because they fit a function early and stop exploring.
numbers: 11 LLMs, mean of 4 runs. Symbolic accuracy vanilla vs with code: GPT-4.1-mini 5.1 to 14.7; GPT-4.1 5.8 to 18.9; o4-mini 47.8 to 45.1; GPT-5-mini 53.1 to 48.1; GPT-5 75.9 to 73.3; Gemini-2.5-flash 50.6 to 40.9; Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4 to 63.7; DeepSeek-R1 43.4 to 37.4; DeepSeek-V3 8.9 to 13.3. GPT-5 on complex systems, hard equations: 40.3 vanilla. Exploration-token rate falls sharply for Gemini-2.5-flash when the code budget goes from 0 to 1. Noise of 0.0001 cuts accuracy 12 to 16%. Mean experiments per task: GPT-4.1 80.6 (accuracy 5.8) vs Gemini-2.5-pro 15.3 (65.4) and Qwen3-235B 8.2.
limits: Exploration rate measured by signature words in reasoning traces, only two models. Code was a free-use tool, not a forced check. Experiment counts are not linked to success within a model. The plausibility-level figure was not readable in extraction.
agent_relevance: Giving the agent code is not the same as forcing a falsifying test. An optional code tool can push the agent into exploitation. Keep code in S7 as a mandatory check, not an open tool.

source: Rios-Garcia et al. (2026) AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically
finding: Across more than 25,000 agent runs in 8 domains, agents rarely treat evidence as a reason to change belief. The base model matters far more than the scaffold. Even injecting near-complete successful traces does not fix hypothesis-driven domains.
numbers: Trace patterns across all configurations: evidence non-uptake 68%; beliefs never updated 71%; refutation-driven belief revision 26%; convergent multi-test evidence 7%; untested claims 53% (63% in hypothesis-driven domains). Non-uptake by domain group: workflow 82%, strategic 66%, hypothesis-driven 60%. Variance explained: base model 41.4%, scaffold 1.5%, environment scope 30.1%. Pass^k falls below 0.05 by k=4 to 6 in spectroscopic structure elucidation and inorganic qualitative analysis. Models include GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-OSS-120B.
limits: Traces were annotated with an LLM-assisted pipeline and a human protocol; models are mid-2025 vintage, not the 2026 frontier. Domains are chemistry-heavy. Scaffolds tested were ReAct and tool-calling only.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 2: the default LLM response to a result is to ignore it, not to discard, patch, or revise it. An explicit contradiction log with a forced decision per anomaly is not covered by the scaffolds tested, so it remains a test, not a finding.

source: Wiemann et al. (2026) DiscoverPhysics, Appendix F failure-mode analysis of Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5
finding: On 22 worlds with altered physics, the strongest agents pass about half. Failures split into never considering the right kind of law (generation), not designing experiments that tell hypotheses apart (selection), and dismissing a contradicting signal as noise (anomaly handling). The two top models fail for different reasons.
numbers: 11 paper worlds, 5 attempts each, 55 runs per model. Opus 4.7 passed 45% (30 failed), GPT-5.5 64% (20 failed). Primary gap per failed run, Opus vs GPT-5.5: consider the right law 6 vs 9; ODE integrator 2 vs 8; design experiments that discriminate hypotheses 8 vs 1; code does not match reasoning 5 vs 0; dismiss a real effect as noise 4 vs 0; act on fitter signals 2 vs 2; know when to stop 3 vs 0. Pipeline layer, Opus vs GPT-5.5 (rows read in table order): execution 8 vs 8, reasoning 10 vs 5, self-monitoring (saw a contradiction, did not act) 8 vs 2, prior knowledge 3 vs 5, perception 1 vs 0. Guided experiments beat randomized ones for Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5; open-source models show no gap. GPT-5.5 'locks in a candidate law early'. Cited from Rios-Garcia: evidence ignored in 68% of traces.
limits: Failure labels were assigned by Claude Opus 4.7, one of the two models analysed (the authors flag this and release outputs). One primary label per run. The layer table lost its row labels in extraction, so the layer split is read by order and is approximate.
agent_relevance: Anomaly handling shows up as two failures: not acting on a contradiction, and calling it noise. For gap 6 in this benchmark, hypothesis class is the bigger miss for GPT-5.5 and experiment choice the bigger miss for Opus, so no single answer holds across models.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) EvoSCM: scientific belief revision through causal model evolution
finding: Keeping beliefs as a small population of explicit causal models, choosing experiments that separate them, and revising by correction rules beats free-form agents on DiscoverPhysics. The two biggest ablation drops are removing the explicit model and removing discriminative experiment choice.
numbers: DiscoverPhysics, explanation score / pass@1: GPT-5.4 baseline 39.80% / 1.86%; EvoSCM 65.30% / 38.08%. GPT-5.5 baseline 51.64% / 7.27%; EvoSCM 75.09% / 56.36%. Ablation (GPT-5.5): w/o SCM (free-form hypotheses) 48.18%; w/o discriminative action (random action) 47.45%; w/o structured revision 70.73%; full 75.09%. Population K=1 63.27%, K=4 74.86%. Baselines GEPA, ReasoningBank, ModelSMC and PiEvo did not beat the plain baseline on explanation (PiEvo 28.18% vs 39.80% on GPT-5.4; 48.18% vs 51.64% on GPT-5.5).
limits: Authors' own method, a preprint; the same group ran all methods. The random-action ablation shows that choosing discriminative tests matters, but it is against random, not against a counterexample prompt or a code-forced check.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a gap 1 answer: tests chosen to separate rival hypotheses matter (47.45 vs 75.09). PiEvo's anomaly module did not transfer to this benchmark.

source: PiEvo (2026) Principle-evolvable scientific discovery via uncertainty minimization (ICML 2026)
finding: Treats high-surprise results as signals to add new principles rather than noise to throw away. Disabling principle expansion hurts; disabling information-directed hypothesis choice also hurts. A think-mode backbone hurt the loop.
numbers: NHO task ablation (Table 6): full 96.36 +/- 1.70 solution quality; w/o hypothesis selection 84.03; w/o principle evolution (static) 85.87. Claimed 29.7% to 31.1% gain over the state of the art on four tasks. Qwen3-14B on MBO: PiEvo 130.01 vs best baseline 67.09 (The-AI-Scientist-v1). Think-mode models degraded performance by about 26.35% in the authors' account.
limits: Authors' tasks and baselines. Another group (EvoSCM, d11) found PiEvo no better than a plain baseline on DiscoverPhysics, so the anomaly-triggered design has not replicated there. The statement that agents 'often discard valid observations as errors' is a claim about prior systems, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Supports building anomaly handling as a trigger (high surprise leads to a new hypothesis class), but treat the size as unproven until tested on others' tasks.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: LLM agent-driven discovery via the scientific method
finding: A naive 'follow the scientific method' prompt let the agent write hypotheses after the fact and explain away unexpected results. A seven-field plan with a numeric prediction written before the code, a falsification criterion, and a forced reconciliation in the next run fixed it in the author's setup.
numbers: Phase 1 (loose prompt, synthetic benchmark): 236 evaluated iterations, 49 consecutive runs with no accepted improvement. After the overhaul: first 11 experiments gave two breakthroughs (0.312 to 0.565 to 0.709); Phase 2: 17 of 64 iterations improved (26.6%). Total 2,151 runs, 229.0M tokens. Final DALE motif finder AUROC 0.842 vs STREME 0.803 on 132 ENCODE factors.
limits: Single independent author, anecdotal. Five fixes were changed at once (real benchmark, scaffold prompt, validator, diagnostics, Kuhn agent), so no ablation isolates the prediction-and-reconcile step.
agent_relevance: Pre-registering a numeric prediction and reconciling it against the result is a cheap way to make an anomaly visible. Worth an A/B at equal tokens.

source: Joshi, Shethia and Lam (2026) SHELDON, Table 5 ablation and baselines re-read
finding: Of the three parts, the separate observation space matters most for diagnosis, comparative analysis and the observation space tie on ARC-AGI-2, and continued exploration matters most for circuit design. No outside group has run SHELDON.
numbers: Ablation (full / w/o comparative analysis / w/o observation space / w/o continued exploration): DiagnosisArena 84.00 / 78.00 / 70.00 / 82.00; ORCA-Bench 66.67 / 56.67 / 53.33 / 53.33; ARC-AGI-2 59.17 / 50.00 / 50.00 / 57.70; QNN topology 1.00 / 0.883 / 0.867 / 0.733. Baselines on the same tasks: ReAct 72.00, 40.00, 25.00, 0.80; Codex 76.00, 40.00, 24.44, 0.82; EvoX ARC-AGI-2 47.50. ARC-AGI-2 under a $2.5 per task budget. All with GPT-5.6-terra at high reasoning.
limits: Authors' tasks only; ORCA steps of 3.3 points suggest about 30 cases. The paper's task count differs by section. No replication found. Which part carries the gain depends on the task.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the store and the comparative analysis are each worth about 6 to 14 points on tasks with anomalies to explain; continued exploration matters where search keeps paying. Replication on third-party tasks is still missing.

source: Land (2026) Modality-driven search with holistic trace judging for ARC-AGI-2: failure analysis
finding: With a pool of up to 29 candidates across text, image and code, the pool already held a correct answer on 86 percent of public-eval instances, yet the final answer was right on 77 percent. Missing hypotheses (generation) were slightly more common than wrong choice (selection).
numbers: ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation, 167 test instances (120 tasks): final 128/167 = 76.65% pass@2; candidate oracle 144/167 = 86.23%. Unsolved 39: 22 generation failures (13.17%; section 6.8 lists 21 plus 1 early-stop failure), 17 selection failures (10.18%). Judge net uplift over majority vote: +7 instances, all minority recoveries. Semi-private set 72.9% at $38.99 per task vs GPT-5.2 Pro 54.2% and Gemini 3 Pro 54.0%. Early-stopped instances (8 candidates) 36 of 37 correct vs 92/130 (70.8%) for full-coverage ones.
limits: One independent author; the ceiling comes from a heavy ensemble (GPT-5.2 x-high plus others), so it shows loss at the top of a large pool, not for a single model. Public-eval contamination unknown. Judge and generator are the same model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: at the frontier with a large pool, generation and selection losses are each about 10 to 13 points. Without a pool, generation is still the first limit (Hypothesis Search, GPT-4: 49 of 100). Measure pool recall and selection accuracy separately.

source: Chen et al. (2025) PhysGym: interactive physics discovery with controlled priors
finding: Prior knowledge usually helps, yet some problems are solved only when context is stripped. Models cut off from names or context are 'paralysed', while those given realistic context can be trapped into conventional forms or realistic test values.
numbers: About 97 environments (inferred from 65.98% = 64/97), four prior levels from L1 (most context) to L4 (anonymised variables). Gemini-2.5-flash success 65.98 / 49.48 / 36.08 / 30.93%; o4-mini 62.89 / 41.24 / 31.96 / 27.84%; experiments per solved task rise from 10.6 to 20.6 (Gemini) and 7.2 to 20.1 (o4-mini). Env 716 solved by Gemini and o4-mini only at L3 and L4; env 409 solved at L1-L2, failed at L3 (conventional 1/r form), solved at L4. Claude 3.7 Sonnet has the largest drop from L3 to L4.
limits: Direct prompting baselines only; non-monotonic counts come from three models; no implausible-true-rule test (the authors list counterfactual physics as future work). Success is binary.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: priors help on average (about 2x from L4 to L1) but can lock in conventional forms on single problems. The agent should vary the amount of context and check whether the answer changes.

source: RAUMA (2026) LLMs can choose what to test, but not what to conclude in active causal discovery (NeurIPS 2026 AI for Science workshop)
finding: When an LLM only picks the intervention and a fixed rule updates the graph, test choice is nearly as good as a simple heuristic. The loss comes when the model has to turn evidence into a conclusion. Supplying the computed statistic nearly closes the gap.
numbers: Active causal discovery with a small intervention budget. The LLM chose the structurally optimal target in 93% of rounds vs 96% for a max-degree heuristic; swapping selectors changed directed-edge F1 by at most 0.025. Letting the LLM restate the graph cost 0.32 F1. Models reversed 55.8% and 46.5% of the arrows the experiments were meant to decide. True children shift 14 to 50 SE, non-children under 2.7. Given one edge and two means, both models decided at chance; stating the rule recovered about a third of the gap; giving the pre-computed z gave 94% vs the rule's 96%.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; the two models are not named there. Causal-graph orientation, not rule discovery. Workshop poster, not peer reviewed in full.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: in this task inference, not test choice, is the larger loss. Make the data-to-decision step code, not model judgment. Contrast with FalsifyBench, where test choice (positive testing) predicted success.

source: Kabra et al. (2026) LLM-AutoSciLab: closed-loop discovery with hypothesis-conditioned acquisition
finding: Choosing observations conditioned on rival hypotheses beats random, uncertainty, plain LLM and code-assisted LLM variants. Removing hypothesis-conditioned acquisition gave a substantial drop on all three benchmarks. Which variable to measure is part of the task.
numbers: ActiveSciBench-GRN (45 tasks): LLM-AutoSciLab exact recovery 31.11% vs LLM-only 0.00%, code-assisted LLM 0.00%, random 2.22%, uncertainty sampling 4.44%. NewtonBench symbolic accuracy 67.6%; ActiveSciBench-Chem 35.1%. Strongest active baselines need 2.60 to 3.10x (NewtonBench), 2.33 to 2.47x (Chem), 3.90 to 4.60x (GRN) queries to match it; LLM-only and code-assisted variants need 5.20 to 14.40x.
limits: Authors' benchmarks (simulator oracles, no real noise or cost). Budget match is in queries, not tokens. Ablation numbers sit in a figure that did not extract.
agent_relevance: Closest to gaps 1 and 9: a code layer that scores candidate experiments against competing hypotheses beats giving the LLM a code tool. The comparison is in queries, so it cannot settle equal-token cost.

source: Shetty and Braga-Neto (2026) LLM-IDEA: identifiability-driven experimental agent
finding: Some failures are not about the agent: the chosen measurements cannot tell the hypotheses apart. A computed identifiability check made this diagnosable. On DiscoverPhysics, models with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade in every non-identifiable world.
numbers: DiscoverPhysics: 15 of 15 model runs with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade in non-identifiable worlds vs 5 of 9 in identifiable ones (p=0.012). ODEBench: 60 of 62 systems with free constants identifiable at round 0; the RC circuit certified exhausted for its protocol. Alien Universe two-body testbed: depth 3 or more on 8/8 seeds with the engine vs 1/8 without.
limits: Authors' own testbed (Alien Universe); a preprint. Shows the observation protocol can be the bottleneck, not that LLMs choose measurements badly by default.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: partial yes. If the available measurements cannot separate the rivals, more search will not help. A step asking what could be measured and whether it separates the rivals is a candidate addition near S4, to be tested before it is added (see section 4b).

source: Agarwal et al. (2026) Evidence-informed LLM beliefs for continual scientific discovery
finding: A discovery loop that rewards belief shift but keeps the model's prior fixed counts many derivative results as surprises. Updating the prior with earlier findings removes about 37.5 percent of the claimed surprises.
numbers: Static surprisals found spurious: 37.5% on average (37.43% in the text); one domain 29.54% and another 25% derivable from earlier findings. Belief-update filtering plus diversity maximisation raises accumulated non-stationary surprisal by 30.62% across five discovery domains.
limits: Measures surprisal against the LLM's own belief, not against ground truth. It speaks to novelty bookkeeping, not directly to how an LLM treats a contradiction.
agent_relevance: An anomaly store should be re-scored against what the agent has learned since, so old anomalies that later got explained are retired, not counted twice.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Auto-Discovery-Bench: state tracking in oracle-guided discovery
finding: With clean deterministic feedback, performance falls as variables, trajectory length and distractors grow. The authors report that many failures stay even when intervention choice and hypothesis generation are removed, pointing to keeping and combining the history as a separate bottleneck.
numbers: Three tasks (directed graph, undirected relational, symbolic equation). On small undirected graphs Grok-4 and Gemini-2.5-pro stay at 100% while GPT-4o drops to 30% and Qwen2.5 to 0% as size grows; with distractors or extra variables most other models are at or below 30% in the easiest cases and fail otherwise. The trajectory-tracking diagnostic is reported as AT-Acc and OA-Acc (full numbers not extracted).
limits: Synthetic, deterministic oracle. The abstract claim is stronger than the numbers read here. Older and smaller models in the table.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 side data: a structured, code-held log of results removes one failure source (the model forgetting or misjoining earlier results) at no extra thinking cost.

source: Hypothesis Search re-check via a 2025 error-source study of LLM hypothesis search for rule induction
finding: A later paper reports that hypothesis search (natural-language hypotheses summarised and implemented as programs) beat direct program generation on list-function rule induction with GPT-4o. Seen only as a search snippet this session.
numbers: Snippet only: about 0.49 mean test accuracy for hypothesis search vs about 0.36 for direct generation (GPT-4o).
limits: Not opened. Search-result snippet only; do not cite the numbers until read. Not run on ARC-AGI-2.
agent_relevance: Would extend Hypothesis Search beyond GPT-4 if confirmed (gap 6).
